title: New delidding tool helps you bake your CPU in the oven to remove heatspreader
summary: Thermal Grizzly just released a CNC-machined CPU delidding tool designed to be placed in an oven after the IHS is loosened.
body: Thermal Grizzly has just added another product to its list of CPU delidding tools: The Delid-Heat-Mate . After loosening the integrated heat spreader (IHS) with the Delid-Die-Mate, you can use the new "Heat-Mate" to hold your CPU, baking it in the oven to allow the solder to melt, before the CPU falls away under its own weight. The tool is compatible with AMD AM5 and Intel LGA 1700/1851/1954 sockets and only costs $23.28, unlike the Delid-Die-Mate Heater that costs $127.41 and is only compatible with Intel LGA 1851 socket CPUs. If you’re serious about chasing lower temperatures and higher performance, delidding your CPU and cooling the die directly is one such way to get there. However, delidding is a scary process, with a real risk of chipping your CPU die or prying off small components under the IHS and turning your CPU into a paperweight. Thermal Grizzly has been at the forefront of making that process easier and less risky with its various delidding tools. The Delid-Die-Mate is the first step in this process, exerting a shear force against the IHS and PCB; you could use the delidding tool alone, but using heat is a less mechanically stressful process. title: Solo developer vibe codes a gallery hosting 36 classic GPU demos
summary: A solo developer known as arkits has created an online gallery to view classic 3D graphics demos live in the browser.
body: Once upon a time, graphics chip vendors made small applications to demonstrate the power of their new hardware. The most accessible were those from 3dfx, ATI Technologies, NVIDIA, and Matrox, since these were the companies dominating PC graphics at the time. If you're nostalgic for that era, you've got to check out this GPU Demo Gallery , because the enterprising creator Archit 'arkits' Khode has ported 36 classic PC graphics card demos to the web, and you can view them right in your browser. The GPU Demo Gallery homepage. You can click through to each demo and view them live in your browser. (Image credit: arkits) It's hard to appreciate from a modern perspective, but in the early 1990s, high-end real-time 3D graphics were largely the domain of specialized workstations costing tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars. By the middle of the decade, companies like 3dfx, Rendition, and VideoLogic ( known for PowerVR ) were promising to bring hardware-accelerated 3D graphics with filtered textures to ordinary PCs at interactive frame rates for a few hundred bucks. It was honestly hard to believe. So what's the simplest way to prove your hardware can do what you say it can? Make a…
